name: Systems
title: Power, noise, batteries and embedded overview
intro: Parts and boards become systems when power, grounding and noise enter the story. These lessons introduce supplies, grounding, noise coupling, EMC intuition, batteries and a map of embedded systems — how hardware and firmware share responsibility.

lessons.title: Power supplies
lessons.summary: Linear vs switching, and clean rails.

sections.p: Circuits need energy at the right voltage. A linear regulator drops excess voltage as heat (simple, quiet). A switching regulator chops and filters to waste less heat (efficient, noisier if poorly laid out).
Linear regulators need Vin above Vout by a dropout margin. An LDO (low dropout) might hold 3.3 V from 3.6 V; an old 7805 needs more headroom above 5 V.
Linear: P ≈ (Vin − Vout) × I. 12 V in to 5 V at 0.5 A wastes ~3.5 W — that needs a heatsink or a rethink toward a buck switcher.
Buck (step-down), boost (step-up), buck-boost… Follow the datasheet layout: short hot loops, recommended inductors/caps. A bad switcher layout radiates noise into everything.

sections.code:
Linear:  Vin --> LDO --> Vout   heat ≈ (Vin-Vout)*I
Buck:    Vin --> switcher+L+C --> Vout  (efficient)

lessons.title: Grounding
lessons.summary: Reference nodes, star points and ground loops.

sections.p: Ground is the reference node your voltages are measured against — not mystical earth magic on a battery gadget. On a PCB it is usually a pour or plane. Poor grounding shows up as noise, resets and "impossible" analog readings.

A star ground joins noisy and sensitive returns at one point. A solid plane is often better for high-speed digital if not shredded by slots. Mixed designs may split analog/digital regions that meet at a single bridge.
Multiple paths between grounded points can pick up interference. Audio systems hum; sensor systems drift. Isolation, careful cabling and single-point bonds are tools.

Mains earth is a safety conductor. Circuit GND may connect to earth through a PSU — or float on a battery. Know which you have before probing with earthed scopes (scope-grounding mistakes are a classic smoke source on mains-referenced gear).
Do not defeat safety earth on mains equipment. Battery-powered learning kits avoid most of these hazards — stay there until you train for mains work.

sections.p: Noise is any unwanted electrical disturbance. It couples by conduction along wires, by electric fields (capacitive coupling), by magnetic fields (inductive coupling), or as radio waves. Debugging starts by asking which path is plausible.
Motors and relays put spikes on shared supplies. Decoupling, separate supplies and snubbers help. Measure at the victim with a scope relative to a sensible ground.
Long parallel wires form accidental transformers and capacitors. Twist pairs, shorten loops, separate sensitive analog from noisy digitals/PWM cables.
0.1 µF near IC power pins handles fast edges; bulk electrolytics/ceramics handle slower demand. Ferrite beads and RC snubbers tame specific bands — measure, don't only sprinkle.

lessons.title: EMC intuition
lessons.summary: Not failing emissions or immunity tests — in spirit.

sections.p: EMC (electromagnetic compatibility) means your device neither emits too much interference nor misbehaves in the presence of interference. Formal testing uses standards; intuition still helps hobby and product design.
Fast edges and large loop areas radiate. Slow edges when you can, small loops, filters on cables, and solid return planes cut emissions. Cables are antennas.
ESD into a connector, radiated RF from a phone, conducted surges on power — design margins, TVS diodes, filtering and watchdog timers improve survival.
You may not own a TEM cell, but you can keep loops small, terminate cables sensibly, and avoid spraying 50 MHz harmonics from a sloppy switcher layout.
Safety isolation and creepage are separate from EMC filters. Mains designs need both — and trained practice. Stay on SELV/low-voltage projects while learning.

practice.why: Don't emit too much; don't wilt from others.

lessons.title: Batteries
lessons.summary: Cells, packs, charging and safe handling.

sections.p: Batteries store chemical energy. Alkaline AA cells are simple for learning. Li-ion/LiPo packs offer high energy density but need proper charge circuits and gentle handling. Warning: shorted or punctured lithium cells can catch fire.
Nominal voltage × amp-hours ≈ watt-hours (rough). A 3.7 V 2 Ah cell is about 7.4 Wh. Capacity depends on discharge rate and temperature.
Lithium cells need CC/CV chargers and usually protection circuits (PCM/BMS). Do not trickle-charge Li-ion like NiMH. Never charge unattended on a flammable surface.
Series adds voltage; parallel adds capacity — but cells must be matched and properly managed. Random parallel of unknown scrap cells is a bad idea.
Store LiPo partly charged in a safe bag/container. Recycle damaged packs at proper facilities — do not bin them in household trash.

sections.p: An embedded system is a computer inside a product: MCU/SoC, sensors, actuators, power and firmware that may run for years. Electronics Learner courses give the hardware vocabulary; firmware makes pins do useful work.
Hardware abstraction → drivers → application logic. Watchdogs reset hung software. Brown-out detectors stop code running at illegal voltages. These features are part of system design.
GPIO, ADC, PWM, UART, SPI, I²C connect the chip to the world. Timing deadlines (motor control, communications) dictate architecture choices — polling vs interrupts vs RTOS.
Power rails correct → clock running → debug probe connects → blink an LED → then talk on a bus. Incremental bring-up beats flashing a full app onto untested hardware.
Schematics, pin tables, power budgets and a README save future-you. Version the firmware with the board revision it expects.

sections.code:
Bring-up ladder:
  1) rails & current limit
  2) reset/clock
  3) SWD/JTAG or UART boot
  4) blink
  5) buses/sensors
  6) application

lessons.title: Decoupling and power integrity
lessons.summary: Keeping rails quiet when chips switch.

sections.p: Power integrity is keeping supply voltage within bounds when currents jump. Decoupling capacitors right at IC power pins supply brief bursts so the rail does not dip each clock edge.
A bulk capacitor (e.g. 10 µF) plus local 100 nF ceramics is a common pattern. The small ceramics handle fast edges; bulk handles longer dips. Follow IC datasheets for recommended counts.
Long thin paths between cap and pins add inductance — the cap "arrives late". Place caps close, use short vias to planes, avoid skinny necks.
Random resets, flaky ADCs, eye diagrams falling apart: sometimes it is software, sometimes the rail is bouncing. Scope VCC at the pins with a short ground spring if you can.

sections.code:
Plane --- via --- VCC pin
              |
            [100n]
              |
Plane --- via --- GND pin   (keep this loop tiny)

options: in series with every data line always
